Log-normal Distribution

The log-normal distributions have been widely used in many different fields such as finance and economics, engineering and reliability, environmental science, medical and biology etc.

If \(X\) follows a lognormal distribution:

\[ f(x; \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{x\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\ln x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right], \quad x > 0 \]

where \(\mu \in \mathbb{R}\) is the mean of \(\ln X\) and \(\sigma^2 > 0\) is the variance of \(\ln X\).

Caution: \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are not population mean and variance of the lognormal distribution!. Instead, we will use \(\mu_{LN}\) and \(\sigma_{LN}^2\) to denote the lognormal mean and variance respectively.

For an i.i.d. random sample \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\):

\[\begin{align*} \ell(\mu, \sigma^2) &= \sum_{i=1}^n \ln f(x_i; \mu, \sigma^2) \\ &= -\frac{n}{2} \ln(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2} \ln \sigma^2 - \sum_{i=1}^n \ln x_i - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\ln x_i - \mu)^2 \end{align*}\]

The \(k\)-th moment of log normal distribution given by

\[ \boxed{ \mathbb{E}[X^k] = \exp\left( k\mu + \frac{1}{2} k^2 \sigma^2 \right). } \]

Particularly, the mean of the above lognormal distribution, denoted by \(\mu_{LN}\), is given by

\[ \mu_{LN} = \mathbb{E}[X] = \exp\left( \mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2 \right). \]

Once the parameters were estimated, say \((\overline{\mu}, \overline{\sigma^2})\), we can use the plug-in Principle to estimate the lognormal mean by

\[ \boxed{\overline{\mu_{LN}} = \exp\left( \overline{\mu} + \frac{1}{2} \overline{\sigma^2} \right).} \]

Working Dataset: A reservoir engineer at an oil exploration company has recently drilled 50 new wells in a shale formation. According to geological theory, the size of oil reserves in this type of formation is often modeled using a log-normal distribution. The engineer is responsible for estimating the typical reserve size and quantifying the uncertainty of these estimates for a presentation to senior management. The estimated ultimate recovery (EUR) for the 50 wells, measured in thousands of barrels (Mbbl), is as follows:

17.3, 24.8, 8.2, 31.5, 14.1, 42.7, 11.9, 55.3, 21.4, 9.7, 36.2, 18.6, 63.1, 13.2, 28.9, 
47.5, 19.8, 7.5, 33.4, 52.1, 16.0, 25.9, 38.7, 10.3, 44.2, 22.5, 58.6, 12.8, 30.3, 48.9, 
20.1, 35.4, 15.7, 60.2, 26.7, 41.3, 18.1, 53.8, 23.9, 46.2, 29.4, 37.6, 14.9, 50.5, 32.8, 
19.3, 56.7, 11.2, 39.5, 27.1

This assignment focuses on finding the asymptotic sampling distributions of the MLE \(\hat{\mu}\) and \(\hat{\sigma^2}\) corresponding to \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) based on an environmental study data.


Question 1: Method of Moments Estimation (MME) of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\)

Estimate the parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) (caution: not \(\sigma\)!) from the raw oil reserve data using the given \(k\)-th moment function. Organize your work into three parts:

  1. Derive the system of two equations for the method of moments estimators (MMEs) of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \mu_1 &=& \exp \left[\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2\right]\\ &=& \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \end{eqnarray*}\] \[\begin{eqnarray*} \mu_2 &=& \exp \left[2\mu + 2 \sigma^2\right]\\ &=& \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 \end{eqnarray*}\]

  1. Derive the closed-form expressions for the MMEs of \(\mu\), \(\sigma^2\), and \(\mu_{LN}\), denoted by \(\widetilde{\mu}\), \(\widetilde{\sigma^2}\), and \(\widetilde{\mu_{LN}}\), respectively.

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \log \mu_2 - 2\log \mu_1 &=& \left( 2 \mu + 2 \sigma^2 \right)- 2\left( \mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\\ &=& \sigma^2 \end{eqnarray*}\] So, \[\widetilde{\sigma^2} = \log \mu_2 - 2\log \mu_1\]


\[\begin{eqnarray*} \log \mu_1 &=& \mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2\\ &\Leftrightarrow&\\ \mu &=& \log \mu_1 - \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2 \\ &=& \log \mu_1 - \frac{1}{2} \left( \log \mu_2 - 2\log \mu_1 \right)\\ &=& 2 \log \mu_1 - \frac{1}{2} \log \mu_2 \end{eqnarray*}\] So, \[\widetilde{\mu} = 2 \log \mu_1 - \frac{1}{2} \log \mu_2\]


plugging in \(\widetilde{\mu}\) and \(\widetilde{\sigma^2}\) to find \(\widetilde{\mu_{LN}}\) \[\begin{eqnarray*} \widetilde{\mu_{LN}} &=& \exp \left(\widetilde{\mu} + \frac{1}{2}\widetilde{\sigma^2}\right)\\ &=& \exp \left[2 \log \mu_1 - \frac{1}{2} \log \mu_2 + \frac{1}{2}\left(\log \mu_2 - 2\log \mu_1\right)\right]\\ &=& \exp \left(2 \log \mu_1 - \frac{1}{2} \log \mu_2 + \frac{1}{2} \log \mu_2 - \log \mu_1 \right)\\ &=& \exp \left(\log \mu_1\right)\\ &=& \mu_1 \end{eqnarray*}\]

  1. Write an R function that outputs the MMEs \(\widetilde{\mu}\), \(\widetilde{\sigma^2}\), and \(\widetilde{\mu_{LN}}\) based on the given data set.
X <- c(17.3, 24.8, 8.2, 31.5, 14.1, 42.7, 11.9, 55.3, 21.4, 9.7, 36.2, 18.6, 63.1, 13.2, 28.9, 
47.5, 19.8, 7.5, 33.4, 52.1, 16.0, 25.9, 38.7, 10.3, 44.2, 22.5, 58.6, 12.8, 30.3, 48.9, 
20.1, 35.4, 15.7, 60.2, 26.7, 41.3, 18.1, 53.8, 23.9, 46.2, 29.4, 37.6, 14.9, 50.5, 32.8, 
19.3, 56.7, 11.2, 39.5, 27.1)

m_1 <- function(X){
  n <- length(X)
  1/n * sum(X)
}

m_2 <- function(X){
  n <- length(X)
  1/n * sum(X^2)
}

sigma_2_tilde <- function(X){
  log(m_2(X)) - 2*log(m_1(X))
}

mu_tilde <- function(X){
  2*log(m_1(X)) - 0.5*log(m_2(X))
}

mu_ln_tilde <- function(X){
  m_1(X)
}

Question 2: Finding the MLE of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\)

This question involves two parts:

(1). Derive the score functions (i.e., the gradient of the log-likelihood) for the parameters of the log-normal distribution, and set them to zero to obtain the system of score equations. Begin with the full log-likelihood and compute its partial derivatives with respect to \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\). [Hint: letting \(\beta = \sigma^2\) may simplify differentiation.]

Assume that \(\{x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n \} \to \text{ LN }(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with density function given by

\[ \ell(\mu, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2} \ln(2\pi) - n \ln \sigma - \sum_{i=1}^n \ln x_i - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\ln x_i - \mu)^2 \]

Score w.r.t \(\mu\)

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \ell(\mu, \sigma^2) &=& \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \left[ -\frac{n}{2} \log (2\pi) - n \log \sigma - \sum_{i=1}^n \log x_i - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right]\\ &=& 0 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\\ &=& \frac{-1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2 \left(\log x_i - \mu \right) \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \left(\log x_i - \mu \right)\\ &=& \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\log x_i - \mu\right)\\ &=& \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \left(-n\mu + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i\right) \end{eqnarray*}\]

Score w.r.t \(\sigma^2\)

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \ell(\mu, \sigma^2)&=& \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \left[ -\frac{n}{2} \log (2\pi) - n \log \sigma - \sum_{i=1}^n \log x_i - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right]\\ &=& \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \left[ -\frac{n}{2} \log (2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log \sigma^2 - \sum_{i=1}^n \log x_i - \frac{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{-1}}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right]\\ &=& -\frac{n}{2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \log \sigma^2 - \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \frac{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{-1}}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\\ &=& - \frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{-2}}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\\ &=& \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left[-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right] \end{eqnarray*}\]
Our gradient of log likelihood \[\nabla \ell(\mu, \sigma^2) = \left\langle \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \left(-n\mu + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i\right) , \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left(-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right)\right\rangle\]

(2). Perform some algebra to find the closed form of the MLE of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\), denoted by \(\widehat{\mu}\) and \(\widehat{\sigma^2}\).

We know extrema will occur when \(\vec{0} = \nabla \ell(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Setting our two score functions equal to zero we get

\[ 0 = \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \left(-n\mu + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i\right)\]

\[0 = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left(-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right)\]

We find

\[\begin{eqnarray*} 0 &=& -n \mu + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i\\ &\Leftrightarrow&\\ n\mu &=& \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i\\ &\Leftrightarrow&\\ \mu &=& \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i}{n} \end{eqnarray*}\]

meaning \[\widehat{\mu} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i}{n}\]

Solving for \(\sigma^2\) \[\begin{eqnarray*} 0 &=& \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left(-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2\right)\\ &\Leftrightarrow&\\ 0 &=& -n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2\\ &\Leftrightarrow&\\ n &=& \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2\\ &\Leftrightarrow&\\ \sigma^2 &=& \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2 \end{eqnarray*}\]

We get our MLE for \(\widehat{\sigma^2}\)

\[\widehat{\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\log x_i - \widehat{\mu}\right)^2\]

(3). Recall that lognormal population mean (i.e., the first moment) is

\[ \mu_{LN} = \mathbb{E}[X] = \exp\left( \mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2 \right). \]

Using the relationship between variance and the first and second moments, \(\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \left(\mathbb{E}[X]\right)^2\), we derive the population variance of the lognormal distribution, denoted as \(\sigma_{\text{LN}}^2\). This result will be used in applying the Central Limit Theorem in subsequent questions

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \sigma_{\text{LN}}^2 &=& \text{Var}[X]\\ &=& \text{E}\left[X^2\right] - \text{E}^2[X]\\ &=& \exp \left(2\mu + 2 \sigma^2\right) - \exp^2 \left(\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2\right)\\ &=& \exp \left(2\mu + 2 \sigma^2\right) - \exp \left(2\mu + \sigma^2\right) \\ &\approx& \exp \left(2 \widehat{\mu} + 2 \widehat{\sigma^2}\right) - \exp \left(2\widehat{\mu} + \widehat{\sigma^2}\right) \end{eqnarray*}\]

Question 3: Sampling Distribution of Lognormal Sample Mean \(\widehat{\mu_{LN}}\)

We have derived two different estimators of lognormal population mean \(\mu_{LN}\). This Question focuses on the sampling distribution of lognormal sample sample means based on MLE. The following are detailed instructions.

(1). Write an R function to estimate the MLE of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\), denoted by \(\widehat{\mu}\) and \(\widehat{\sigma^2}\) and return the MLE of \(\mu_{LN}\), denoted by \(\widehat{\mu_{LN}}\).

mu_hat <- function(X){
  n <- length(X)
  sum(log(X)) / n
}

sigma_2_hat <- function(X){
    n <- length(X)
    mu <- mu_hat(X)
    sum((log(X) - mu)^2) / n
}

mu_ln_hat <- function(X){
  exp(mu_hat(X) + 0.5 * sigma_2_hat(X))
}

\(\widehat{\mu}\) = 3.2685359
\(\widehat{\sigma^2}\) = 0.3271989
\(\widehat{\mu_{LN}}\) = 30.9426444

(2). Take 1000 Bootstrap samples from the raw oil data set. For each bootstrap sample, call the above R function to find the bootstrap MLE of \(\mu_{LN}\), denoted by \(\widehat{\mu_{LN}^*}^{(1)}, \widehat{\mu_{LN}^*}^{(2)}, \cdots, \widehat{\mu_{LN}^*}^{(1000)}\).

boostrap_sample_iteration <- function(X,  estimator){
  sample_i <- sample(X, size=length(X), replace=TRUE)
  estimator(sample_i)
}

#create replicant_n replicant samples
replicant_n <- 1000

#simplify=TRUE param gives us vector as output
bootstrap_estimator_dist <- replicate(n=replicant_n, expr=boostrap_sample_iteration(X, mu_ln_hat), simplify=TRUE)

(3). Using kernel density estimation approach to estimate the bootstrap density curves based on the bootstrap MLEs: \(\widehat{\mu_{LN}^*}^{(1)}, \widehat{\mu_{LN}^*}^{(2)}, \cdots, \widehat{\mu_{LN}^*}^{(1000)}\).

ggplot(data=data.frame(x=bootstrap_estimator_dist)) + 
  geom_density(aes(x=x, color="Kernel Estimate")) +
  labs(title="Gaussian Kernel Estimate of Bootstrap Distribution", x=expression(widehat(mu)[LN]), y="Density") + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

(4). In order to find the asymptotic sampling distribution using the central limit theorem (CLT). That is, when sample size is large,

\[ \bar{X} \to N \left(\mu_{LN}, \frac{\sigma_{LN}}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \]

where \(\mu_{LN}\) and \(\sigma_{LN}\) can be estimated by using the plug-in principle of MLE. Based on the asymptotic sampling distribution of lognormal sample mean \(\bar{X}\), add the asymptotic density curve to the above Bootstrap kernel density curve.

horizontal_points <- seq(min(bootstrap_estimator_dist)-1, max(bootstrap_estimator_dist)+1, length.out=replicant_n)

sigma_2_ln_hat <- exp(2 * mu_hat(X) + 2 * sigma_2_hat(X)) - mu_ln_hat(X)^2 
ggplot(data=data.frame(x=bootstrap_estimator_dist,
                       x_asym=horizontal_points, 
                       y_asym=dnorm(horizontal_points, mean=mu_ln_hat(X), sd=sqrt(sigma_2_ln_hat / length(X))))) + 
  geom_density(aes(x=x, color="Bootstrap Kernel Estimate")) + 
  geom_line(aes(x=x_asym, y=y_asym, color="Asymptotic Normal")) + 
  labs(title="sampling distributions of lognormal sample mean", x=expression(bar(X)), y="Density") + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

(5). Write a short summary to compare the two sampling distributions of the sample mean of the lognormal distribution.
Here our two estimations appear very close visually. Both are symmetrical and normal shaped, and both are centered at the same location. The primary difference appears around the tails and peak. These locations show the KDE’s roughness.

Question 4: Extra Bonus Credit

Derive the Hessian matrix by computing the second-order partial derivatives of the log-likelihood function (with respect to \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\)). Then, translate the derived Hessian into an R function that takes the MLEs of the parameters and the data as inputs and returns the Hessian matrix. Finally, compare your analytically derived Hessian with the numerical Hessian returned by optim().


We wish to find the second order partial derivatives of the score
Starting with \(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \mu^2} \ell (\mu, \sigma^2)\) \[\begin{eqnarray*} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \mu^2} \ell (\mu, \sigma^2) &=& \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \left(-n\mu + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i\right)\\ &=& \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \left(-n\mu + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i\right)\\ &=& \frac{-n}{\sigma^2} \end{eqnarray*}\]
Next \(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial (\sigma^2)^2} \ell(\mu, \sigma^2)\) \[\begin{eqnarray*} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial (\sigma^2)^2} \ell(\mu, \sigma^2) &=& \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2}\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left(-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right)\\ &=&\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \left(-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right) +\left(-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right) \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\\ &=& \frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} \left(0 + \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2 \right) + \left(-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right) \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\\ &=& \frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} \left(\frac{-1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2 \right) + \left(-n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log x_i - \mu)^2\right) \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \left(\frac{-1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^2}\right)\\ &=& \frac{-1}{2\left(\sigma^2\right)^2} \left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2 - n + \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2\right)\\ &=& \frac{-1}{2\left(\sigma^2 \right)^2} \left(-n + \frac{2}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2 \right)\\ &=& \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2 \right)^2} \left(\frac{n}{2} - \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2 \right)\\ \end{eqnarray*}\]

Next, \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \ell(\mu, \sigma^2)\)

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \ell(\mu, \sigma^2) &=& \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \left(-n \mu + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i \right)\\ &=& \frac{-1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^2 }\left(-n \mu + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i \right)\\ &=& \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^2 }\left(n \mu - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i \right) \end{eqnarray*}\]

Since \(\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \sigma^2 \partial \mu}\) is continuous on it’s domain, Schwarz’s theorem implies that \(\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \sigma^2 \partial \mu} = \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \mu \partial \sigma^2}\)

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal{H}(\mu, \sigma^2)&=& \nabla \left(\nabla \ell\right)^T\\ &=& \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma^2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial\mu} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \sigma^2}\\ \end{pmatrix}\\ &=& \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \mu^2} & \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \mu \partial \sigma^2}\\ \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \sigma^2 \partial \mu} & \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \sigma^2} \end{pmatrix}\\ &=& \begin{pmatrix} \frac{-n}{\sigma^2} & \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^2 }\left(n \mu - \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i \right)\\ \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^2 }\left(n \mu - \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log x_i \right) & \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2 \right)^2} \left(\frac{n}{2} - \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\log x_i - \mu \right)^2 \right) \end{pmatrix} \end{eqnarray*}\]

H <- function(mu_mle, sigma_2_mle, X){
  n <- length(X)
  mu_mu <- -n / sigma_2_mle
  mu_sigma_2 <- (1/ sigma_2_mle^2) * (n * mu_mle - sum(log(X)))
  sigma_2_sigma_2 <- (1/ sigma_2_mle^2) * (n/2 - (1/sigma_2_mle) * sum((log(X)-mu_mle)^2))
  matrix(c(mu_mu, mu_sigma_2, mu_sigma_2, sigma_2_sigma_2), 2, 2, byrow=TRUE)
}

H(mu_hat(X), sigma_2_hat(X), X)
          [,1]      [,2]
[1,] -152.8123    0.0000
[2,]    0.0000 -233.5158
lognormal_density <- function(X, mu, sigma_2){
  #abuse normal distribution density for lognormal
  (1/X) * dnorm(log(X), mean=mu, sd=sqrt(sigma_2))
}

lognormal_score <- function(X){
  function(params){
    mu <- params[1]
    sigma_2 <- params[2]
    sum(log(lognormal_density(X, mu, sigma_2)))
  }
}

score_grad <- function(X){
  n <- length(X)
  A <- sum(log(X))
  function(params){
    mu <- params[1]
    sigma_2 <- params[2]
    score_wrt_mu <- (1/sigma_2) * (-n * mu + A)
    score_wrt_sigma_2 <- (1/2/sigma_2) * (-n + (1/sigma_2) * sum((log(X) - mu)^2))
    c(score_wrt_mu, score_wrt_sigma_2)
  }
}

score <- lognormal_score(X)
gradient_of_score <- score_grad(X)

critial_value <- optim(
  par=c(3.26,  0.327), #guess close to analytic solution
  fn=score,
  gr=gradient_of_score,
  method="L-BFGS-B",
  hessian=TRUE,
  #same control list from lecture notes
  control = list(trace = FALSE,
                 fnscale = -1, #swap minimization for maximization
                 maxit = 500,
                 abstol = 1e-8)
)
